citation.title: Changing Climates of Conflict: A Social Network Experiment in 56 Schools

standing_assumptions:
The article (PNAS 113(3):566–571; printed pp. 566–571 are main PDF pp. 1–6) and its SI Appendix (43 pages; the printed page number equals the supplement PDF page number) state no theorem, proposition or lemma and give no proof. Their formal objects are the school-level regressions (SI Eqs. (1)–(6)), the exposure mapping, the exposure probabilities and the inverse-probability-weighted regression estimator (SI pp. 16–19), one sentence of asymptotic justification (SI p. 19) and the notes to Tables S6 and S7. There are two official corrections: PNAS 115(15):E3598 (2018), which replaces 30% by 25%, and a 2019 correction that adds a grant number. Everything quoted below was read from the rendered page images.
(S1) Schools and blocks. SI p. 5 (Study design): “Prior to randomization, schools agreed to participate in all measurement aspects of the program, with a 50% chance of receiving the anti-conflict program (the treatment).” “Schools were assigned to blocks of four, and randomized to receive the treatment or not within these blocks.” “Four schools dropped out from the study before the point of randomization, which left the total sample at 56 schools and 24,191 students.” Fig. S1, caption (SI p. 24): “The 56 schools were first blocked into groups of four by pretreatment school level variables including size and student demographics (see SI). Within each of the 14 school blocks, two schools were assigned to control (the two school networks on the left), and two to treatment, the anti-conflict intervention (the two school networks on the right). The nodes depict the population of students at the school. Grey nodes are the “seed eligible” students, selected by a deterministic algorithm and comprising a representative sample of the school. Seed eligibles were blocked into four equally sized groups based on pretreatment characteristics including gender and grade, and half of the students in each block were randomly assigned to be treated (part of the anti-conflict program) if they were in a treatment school; dark green nodes are treated seed eligibles. Nodes in the shape of stars are the social referents, who are in the top 10% of their school in connections reported by other students in the pre-randomization survey.”
(S2) Seed-eligibles and seeds. SI p. 6, with $a_i$ a student's indegree and $b_i$ the student's closure: “The students in each of the gender-grade-$b_i$ blocks with the largest values of $a_i$ were considered eligible for randomization into the seed group, such that we had no fewer than 40 seed-eligible students (schools with fewer than 200 students), and no more than 64 seed-eligible students (schools with less than 550 students). For schools with between 200 and 550, we scaled linearly between 40 and 64 seed-eligible students, rounding to the nearest 4. Table S2 demonstrates the covariate profiles of eligible and ineligible students. All of our estimates are computed conditional on the composition of the seed-eligible groups. Among treated schools, half of the seed-eligibles were block-randomized into the seed group, using 4 blocks constructed using gender, grade, and $b_i$ (using an R package, blockTools).” Main p. 567 (PDF p. 2): “In the 28 of 56 schools randomly assigned to receive the intervention, we selected a group of students (the seed-eligibles) using a deterministic algorithm (see SI Appendix for materials and methods used) designed to represent 15% of the school population, blocked by gender and grade and capped at 64 students (grades ranged from 5 to 8) (SI Appendix, Figs. S1 and S2, and Table S1). We randomly assigned 50% of that group (the seeds) to be invited to participate in the anticonflict intervention, which our team implemented over the course of the school year. Within each seed group at each school (on average 26 seeds at each school, for a total of 728 seeds across 28 schools), a random proportion were social referent seeds, meaning they were in the top 10% of their school in the number of connections reported by other students (i.e., indegree).”
(S3) School-level (climate) regressions. SI p. 13: “We fit the following linear regression model: $Y_{ij} = \alpha_j + \tau D_{ij} + \gamma C^E_{ij} + u_{ij}$ (1) where $ij$ denotes the $i$th school in the $j$th block. $Y_{ij}$ denotes school-level outcomes, $\alpha_j$ is a block-level fixed effect, $D_{ij}$ is the school-level treatment assignment, $C_{ij}$ is the composition of the seed group (percentage of seed group that is classified as a social referent), and $C^E_{ij}$ is the composition of the seed eligible group (percentage of seed eligible group that is classified as a social referent). $\tau$ here is the average causal effect of treatment. We include $C^E_{ij}$ as a covariate control here so as to maximize comparability with the interaction model in (4). In all cases, the model is fit with OLS regression with heteroskedasticity-robust standard errors to characterize uncertainty.” The interaction model, Eq. (2) (repeated as Eq. (4)), and its interpretation are transcribed in P037-T14. SI p. 16: “This amounts to fitting the following model for main effects: $Y_{ij} = \alpha_j + \tau D_{ij} + \gamma C^E_{ij} + \boldsymbol{\theta}\mathbf{X}_{ij} + u_{ij}$, (5) where $\mathbf{X}_{ij}$ is a vector of school-specific pretreatment covariates (percentage white, percentage English-speaking, average house quality and, where available, pretreatment measurement of $Y_{ij}$).” Main p. 568 (PDF p. 3): “We computed confidence intervals and P values using robust SEs under a normal approximation.” Main p. 567: “(Administrative data were available for 49 of the 56 schools, and we restricted our attention to these schools for analyses of conflict-related events.)”
(S4) Scale of composition. In the targets $C_{ij}$ and $C^E_{ij}$ are fractions in $[0,1]$ (0.20 means 20%), the scale of Fig. 2 and Table S7. The SI's wording (“percentage”, “$c\%$”, “percentage points”) does not match that scale; this is finding P037-N020, rated a clarity note, and is not a target.
(S5) Social-influence setting. SI pp. 16–17: “We have a finite population of students indexed by $i = 1, ..., N$ on which our randomized experiment is performed. Define a treatment assignment vector, $\mathbf{z} = (z_1, ..., z_N)'$, where $z_i \in \{0, 1\}$ denotes whether or not student $i$ is assigned to be a seed (i.e., is invited to participate in the anti-conflict group). An experimental design is a plan for randomly selecting a particular value of $\mathbf{z}$ with predetermined probability $p_{\mathbf{z}}$. Restricting our attention only to treatment assignments that can be generated by our experimental design, define $\Omega = \{\mathbf{z} : p_{\mathbf{z}} > 0\}$, so that $\mathbf{Z} = (Z_1, ..., Z_N)'$ is a random vector with support $\Omega$ and $\Pr(\mathbf{Z} = \mathbf{z}) = p_{\mathbf{z}}$. In this setting, treatment assignment is the random assignment of seeds both across and within schools according our hierarchical randomization (i.e., so that half of schools are assigned to control schools with no seeds).” The exposure mapping $f(\mathbf{z},\theta_i)$ with $\theta_i$, $\gamma$ and $s_i$ (SI p. 17) is transcribed in P037-T7. SI p. 18: “We allow for each student $i$ to have a vector of potential outcomes, which we denote by $(y_i(d_C), ...y_i(d_D))$, that do not depend on the value of $\mathbf{Z}$. We seek estimates for $k \in \{C, S, NI, I\}$ (i.e., control exposure, school exposure, non-social referent peer exposure, social referent peer exposure) of the average potential outcome $\mu(d_k) = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N} y_i(d_k)$.” “$\pi_i(d_k) = \sum_{\mathbf{z}\in\Omega} \mathbf{I}(f(\mathbf{z},\theta_i) = d_k)\Pr(\mathbf{Z} = \mathbf{z})$.” “We restrict ourselves to the subpopulation of students (n=2451) for which there exists some probability that students could receive all four exposures: $0 < \pi_i(d_k) < 1$ for $k \in \{C, S, NI, I\}$.” The estimator $\widehat{\mu_R}(d_k)$ (SI p. 19) is transcribed in P037-T11.
(S6) None of the eleven headline claims (P037-H1 to P037-H11) is a mathematical statement: each is an empirical estimate, a description of the design or an interpretive conclusion. Every target below therefore comes from a confirmed error.
(S7) [Added on 6 October 2026, after the authors' analysis code became available; it applies to the revised P037-T2 and to P037-T18 onward.] The authors' eleven R scripts, as released by ICPSR with study 37070, were not available when (S1)–(S6) and P037-T1 to T17 were written. In the targets added or revised afterwards, ‘the released code’ means those scripts as read and run by the checkers; a statement of what the code does is established by the code and is not a statement of the publication. ‘On the public data’ means a value obtained from the public data release (ICPSR 37070 V2) run through the authors' scripts with an adapter, or from a reconstruction on that release; the authors' own analysis files are not public and ICPSR states that some variables in the release were changed, so such a value is not the value the authors would obtain from their own files. No such value is part of a target's statement: the statements are exact identities, probabilities, counts and counterexamples, and values on the public data appear only in notes, as aggregates (the data are respondent-level records of school students; no respondent row and no school identifier is given). The scripts are cited by number: script 1, ‘1. Sanitize and generate perms, probs.R’ (the network, referent status, the simulated seed and school assignments, the exposure indicators and their simulated probabilities); script 2, ‘2. Cleaning.R’ (outcomes and covariates); script 3, ‘3. Network results.R’ (the social-influence estimates and their randomization standard errors); script 4, ‘4. School results-with-correction.R’ (the school-level regressions, their three kinds of standard error, the percentages of the 2018 Correction and Fig. 2); script 6, ‘6. Bond et al analysis.R’ (Fig. S5). Line numbers are those of the released files, as cited by the checkers.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: SI Appendix, the asymptotic justification of the social-influence estimator, corrected: consistency and asymptotic normality along a growing sequence of independently randomized four-school blocks
canonical_claim.statement:
[Printed] The sentence is transcribed in P037-T10. [Sol's corrected text (validated.json, P037-E004, prior_correction.corrected_text), verbatim] “Schools within each four-school randomization block are dependent. With independently randomized blocks, consistency and asymptotic normality can be justified along a growing sequence of blocks under block-level LLN and Lindeberg conditions and appropriate regularity for the fitted regression and estimated exposure probabilities. This repair does not itself imply a change in a constant-effect variance calculation that uses the actual blocked randomization.” [Sol's smallest repair, verbatim] “Replace the asserted independent-school construction with independently randomized four-school block totals and apply LLN/Lindeberg conditions to those totals. For the fitted estimator, supply regression regularity and negligible exposure-probability simulation error or an appropriate joint asymptotic argument. Keep the same retained-population estimand and treatment design.”
[Mathematical content: the validator's sufficient argument.] For each $B = 1, 2, \dots$ there are $B$ randomization blocks. Fixed for each $B$: the schools, networks, covariates, potential outcomes, seed-eligible sets and the retained set of students. The randomizations of different blocks (of schools within the block, and of seeds within its schools) are independent, and the exposure of a student is a function of the randomization of that student's block only; dependence inside a block is unrestricted. Let $S_b$ be the retained students of block $b$, $N_B = \sum_{b=1}^{B}|S_b|$, fix an exposure $d_k$, and write $I_i = \mathbf{1}\{D_i = d_k\}$, $\pi_i = \Pr(I_i = 1) > 0$, $y_i = y_i(d_k)$. For deterministic numbers $g_i$ put
$$h_i = g_i + \frac{I_i}{\pi_i}\,(y_i - g_i),\qquad X_b = \sum_{i \in S_b}h_i,\qquad \tilde\mu_B = \frac1{N_B}\sum_{b=1}^{B}X_b,\qquad \mu_B = \frac1{N_B}\sum_{b=1}^{B}\sum_{i \in S_b}y_i .$$
Assume constants $m, c, \eta, K$ not depending on $B$, with $c > 0$ and $|S_b| \le m$, $N_B \ge cB$, $\pi_i \ge \eta > 0$, $|y_i| \le K$ and $|g_i| \le K$.
(1) $\mathrm{E}[h_i] = y_i$, so $\mathrm{E}[X_b] = \sum_{i \in S_b}y_i$ and $\mathrm{E}[\tilde\mu_B] = \mu_B$.
(2) $X_1, \dots, X_B$ are independent.
(3) $|h_i| \le H := K + 2K/\eta$, $|X_b| \le mH$ and $\mathrm{Var}(X_b) \le m^2H^2$.
(4) $\mathrm{Var}(\tilde\mu_B) = N_B^{-2}\sum_b\mathrm{Var}(X_b) \le \dfrac{m^2H^2}{c^2B}$.
(5) [Consistency.] $\Pr(|\tilde\mu_B - \mu_B| > \varepsilon) \le \dfrac{m^2H^2}{c^2B\,\varepsilon^2} \to 0$ for every $\varepsilon > 0$.
(6) [Asymptotic normality.] If in addition $s_B^2 := \sum_b\mathrm{Var}(X_b) \ge \sigma_0^2B$ for a constant $\sigma_0^2 > 0$, then with $U_b = X_b - \mathrm{E}[X_b]$ one has $|U_b| \le 2mH$, so $\dfrac1{s_B^2}\sum_b\mathrm{E}[U_b^2\,\mathbf{1}\{|U_b| > \varepsilon s_B\}] = 0$ as soon as $\varepsilon\sqrt{\sigma_0^2B} > 2mH$ (the Lindeberg condition), and $\sum_bU_b/s_B = N_B(\tilde\mu_B - \mu_B)/s_B$ converges in distribution to $N(0,1)$.
(7) [Contrasts.] The same holds for a contrast of two exposures $d_k$, $d_l$, with $h_i$ replaced by the difference of the two corresponding terms, the bound $H$ doubled and the variance condition imposed on the contrast's block totals; no independence between the two exposure-specific estimates is needed.
(8) [Fitted regression and simulated probabilities.] Let $\mathbf{x}_i$ be deterministic vectors of fixed dimension and bounded norm, and for a coefficient vector $\beta$ and positive weights $p = (p_i)$ write $\hat\mu(\beta,p) = N_B^{-1}\sum_i[\mathbf{x}_i'\beta + \tfrac{I_i}{p_i}(y_i - \mathbf{x}_i'\beta)]$, so that $\tilde\mu_B = \hat\mu(\beta,\pi)$ when $g_i = \mathbf{x}_i'\beta$. Then, exactly, for all $\hat\beta$, $\beta_*$ and all positive $\hat\pi_i$: $\hat\mu(\hat\beta,\pi) - \hat\mu(\beta_*,\pi) = \big[N_B^{-1}\sum_i(1 - \tfrac{I_i}{\pi_i})\mathbf{x}_i\big]'(\hat\beta - \beta_*)$ and $\hat\mu(\hat\beta,\hat\pi) - \hat\mu(\hat\beta,\pi) = N_B^{-1}\sum_iI_i\,(y_i - \mathbf{x}_i'\hat\beta)\,(\hat\pi_i^{-1} - \pi_i^{-1})$. If in addition $N_B^{-1}\sum_i\mathbf{x}_i\mathbf{x}_i' \to Q$ positive definite and $N_B^{-1}\sum_i\mathbf{x}_iy_i \to v$, with $\beta_* = Q^{-1}v$, if $\hat\beta = \big(\sum_i\tfrac{I_i}{\hat\pi_i}\mathbf{x}_i\mathbf{x}_i'\big)^{-1}\sum_i\tfrac{I_i}{\hat\pi_i}\mathbf{x}_iy_i$ on samples with nonsingular weighted Gram matrix (set $\hat\beta=0$ on singular samples), and if $\max_i|\hat\pi_i - \pi_i| = o_p(B^{-1/2})$, then $\hat\beta \to \beta_*$ in probability and $\hat\mu(\hat\beta,\hat\pi) - \hat\mu(\beta_*,\pi) = o_p(B^{-1/2})$; hence the consistency conclusion of (5) holds for the fitted estimator $\hat\mu(\hat\beta,\hat\pi)$, and the distributional limit in (6) also holds under its variance condition with $g_i = \mathbf{x}_i'\beta_*$.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed:
The estimator, SI p. 19: “For covariate adjustment, define an estimated parameter vector associated with exposure condition $d_k$
$$\widehat\xi(d_k) = \arg\min_{\xi(d_k)}\sum_{i : D_i = d_k}\frac{1}{\pi_i(d_k)}\left[y_i(d_k) - g(\mathbf{x_i},\xi(d_k))\right]^2,$$
where $g(.)$ is the specification for the regression of $y_i(d_k)$ on $\mathbf{x_i}$. $\xi(d_k)$ is the parameter vector arising from an inverse probability weighted regression of outcomes on covariates among students in a given level of exposure. Then the regression estimator for the mean is
$$\widehat{\mu_R}(d_k) = \frac{1}{N_s}\sum_{i : \pi_i(d_k) > 0,\ \forall k \in \{C,S,NI,I\}}\left[\mathbf{I}(D_i = d_k)\,\frac{y_i(d_k) - g\big(\mathbf{x_i},\widehat\xi(d_k)\big)}{\hat\pi_i(d_k)} + g\big(\mathbf{x_i},\widehat\xi(d_k)\big)\right],$$
where $N_s$ denotes the number of students such that $0 < \pi_i(d_k) < 1$ for all $i$ and for $k \in \{C, S, NI, I\}$.” “Estimation of average causal effects follows using a plug-in estimate, $\hat\mu_R(d_k) - \hat\mu_R(d_l)$.” $D_i = f(\mathbf{Z},\theta_i)$ is the exposure of student $i$, $\pi_i(d_k)$ its probability and $\hat\pi_i(d_k)$ its simulated estimate (SI pp. 17–18; P037-T9); potential outcomes $y_i(d_k)$ are fixed (standing assumption (S5)). In the validator's notation $\tilde\mu_B$ is this estimator with known probabilities and fixed predictions $g_i$ (the retained students playing the role of the $N_s$ students), and (8) passes to the fitted linear specification $g(\mathbf{x}_i,\xi) = \mathbf{x}_i'\xi$ and the estimated probabilities. A block is one of the four-school randomization blocks of standing assumption (S1). All conditions on $m, c, \eta, K, \sigma_0^2, Q$ are the validator's sufficient conditions and are not in the paper, which already restricts to students with $0 < \pi_i(d_k) < 1$ (pointwise positivity).
canonical_claim.finite_lemmas: Exact, for each fixed $B$ (P037-E004/v1/artifact/derivation.md, ‘Why grouping into blocks can repair the argument’ and ‘Fitted regression and simulated probabilities’): (1) unbiasedness, from $\mathrm{E}[I_i] = \pi_i$; (2) independence of block totals, each being a function of its own block's randomization; (3) the bounds $|h_i| \le |g_i| + |y_i - g_i|/\pi_i \le K + 2K/\eta$, $|X_b| \le mH$, $\mathrm{Var}(X_b) \le \mathrm{E}[X_b^2] \le m^2H^2$; (4) the variance identity and bound; (5) Chebyshev's inequality with the explicit bound $m^2H^2/(c^2B\varepsilon^2)$; in (6) the bound $|U_b| \le 2mH$, by which every term of the Lindeberg sum vanishes once $\varepsilon\sqrt{\sigma_0^2B} > 2mH$; in (8) the two exact subtraction identities, and the fact that each component of $N_B^{-1}\sum_i(1 - I_i/\pi_i)\mathbf{x}_i$ has mean $0$ and variance $O(1/B)$. The finite facts about dependence within a block are P037-T10. The limit statements use the Lindeberg–Feller central limit theorem for independent triangular arrays and Slutsky's theorem.
canonical_claim.note: Repair cost: minor_regularity_condition. The corrected sentence itself is a statement that a justification exists ‘under block-level LLN and Lindeberg conditions and appropriate regularity’; the mathematical content above is the validator's one explicit set of sufficient conditions, which are stated as sufficient and not as necessary, and are not verified for any sequence that contains the actual 56 schools. In (6) the validator's constant $v$ for the variance lower bound is renamed $\sigma_0^2$, because $v$ is also used in (8). (8) is given in the validator's artifact for a fixed-dimensional linear regression fitted on the retained population; the paper's $g(.)$ is not specified further. Not established: that the paper's estimator is inconsistent, or that the reported constant-effect randomization variances are wrong; the repair ‘does not itself imply a change in a constant-effect variance calculation that uses the actual blocked randomization’.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: SI Appendix, Study design, the size of the seed-eligible group: ‘no more than 64 seed-eligible students (schools with less than 550 students)’, corrected
canonical_claim.location: SI Appendix p. 6 (supplement PDF p. 6); the related sentence is on main p. 567 (PDF p. 2)
canonical_claim.statement:
[Printed, SI p. 6] “The students in each of the gender-grade-$b_i$ blocks with the largest values of $a_i$ were considered eligible for randomization into the seed group, such that we had no fewer than 40 seed-eligible students (schools with fewer than 200 students), and no more than 64 seed-eligible students (schools with less than 550 students). For schools with between 200 and 550, we scaled linearly between 40 and 64 seed-eligible students, rounding to the nearest 4.” [Sol's smallest repair (validated.json, P037-E008), verbatim] “Replace the upper-cap parenthesis by “schools with at least 550 students”. For explicit endpoints: 40 for size at most 200; 64 for size at least 550; interpolate and round to the nearest multiple of four between them. No required change to the main-text design-intent wording.”
[Mathematical content.] For a school of $n$ students ($n$ a positive integer) let the number of seed-eligible students be
$$e(n) = \begin{cases}40, & n \le 200,\\ 4\cdot\mathrm{round}\!\Big(\dfrac{1}{4}\Big(40 + 24\,\dfrac{n - 200}{350}\Big)\Big), & 200 < n < 550,\\ 64, & n \ge 550,\end{cases}$$
where $\mathrm{round}$ is rounding to the nearest integer.
(i) For an integer $n$ the number $\tfrac14(40 + 24\tfrac{n-200}{350}) = 10 + \tfrac{3(n-200)}{175}$ is never half an odd integer, so no tie rule is needed.
(ii) For every $n$: $40 \le e(n) \le 64$, $e(n)$ is a multiple of 4, and $e$ is nondecreasing.
(iii) [The corrected parenthesis.] $e(n) = 64$ for every $n \ge 550$, and the linear scale $40 + 24\tfrac{n-200}{350}$ equals 40 at $n = 200$ and 64 at $n = 550$.
(iv) [The printed parenthesis fails.] Schools with less than 550 students do not all have 64 seed-eligible students: $e(100) = 40$, $e(200) = 40$ and $e(375) = 52$. Exactly, $e(n) = 64$ if and only if $n \ge 521$.
(v) [The share is not constant.] $e(n)/n$ equals $\tfrac25$, $\tfrac15$, $\tfrac{52}{375}$, $\tfrac{64}{550}$ and $\tfrac{64}{715}$ at $n = 100, 200, 375, 550, 715$.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: $a_i$ is a student's indegree and $b_i$ the student's closure (SI p. 6); the seed-eligible students of a school are those from whom the seeds are drawn (standing assumption (S2)). The function $e$ is the rule of the two printed sentences with Sol's endpoints (‘40 for size at most 200; 64 for size at least 550; interpolate and round to the nearest multiple of four between them’); the paper does not give it a symbol. Main p. 567: the seed-eligible group was ‘designed to represent 15% of the school population, blocked by gender and grade and capped at 64 students’. Table S1 (SI p. 36) has a block whose mean school size is 715.00, so schools above 550 students occur.
canonical_claim.note: P037-E008 is rated an error, Minor (ratings.json): a misprint in the parenthesis that says where the cap of 64 is reached. Sol's verdict is confirmed in part (batch validation); evidence type recalculation_from_source, so there is no counterexample target; the values in (iv) and (v) are those of P037-B01/work/checks.py. Repair cost: none. A marginal target: a slip in the prose description of a design rule, included because the rule is an explicit piecewise formula, the printed range is false for it and the author's instruction covers every confirmed mathematical error at any severity. Sol's repair names ‘at least 550’ as the range where the cap applies by rule; (iv) records that, after rounding to the nearest 4, the value 64 is already reached from $n = 521$. Not established: any error in the eligible groups actually formed, and the school-average share of about 15% (the roster data are not staged); Sol finds no defect in the main text's ‘designed to represent 15%’ read as a design aim. (i)–(v) were recomputed for $1 \le n < 1000$ when this list was fixed.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Results, second paragraph: ‘each student was disciplined on average 0.08 times during the year’ when 20% of the group are social referent seeds, corrected to about 0.095
canonical_claim.location: main p. 569 (PDF p. 4), with Fig. 2D on the same page; SI Table S7, p. 42 (supplement PDF p. 42)
canonical_claim.statement:
[Printed, main p. 569] “When 20% of a treatment school's anticonflict group is composed of social referent seeds (proportions ranged from 0 to 37%), we estimate that each student was disciplined on average 0.08 times during the year, a reduction of 60% compared with control schools and twice the average effect of the anticonflict groups.” [Printed, Table S7, column Peer conflict] School effect with 0% Social Referents: $0.04$; Interaction: Proportion of Referents in Treatment group: $-0.85$.
[Sol's smallest repair (validated.json, P037-N010), verbatim] “Replace ‘on average 0.08 times’ at 20% referents with ‘on average about 0.095 times’ (or about 0.10 to two decimals), using Figure 2D's adjusted predictions. A clearer complete description uses about 0.223 for the fitted control level, about 57% for the reduction, and roughly 2.2 times the average decrease. In the amended first paragraph, label 0.20 as unadjusted and state that 25% uses an adjusted control mean about 0.226; retain the corrected 25%.”
[Mathematical content.] In the interaction model (SI Eqs. (4), (6)) the estimated effect of treatment at seed-group fraction $c$ is $\Delta(c) = \hat\tau_0 + \hat\beta c$, and the predicted level in a treatment school is $m_1(c) = m_0 + \Delta(c)$, where $m_0$ is the fitted control level.
(i) With the printed coefficients, $\Delta(0.20) = 0.04 + (-0.85)(0.20) = -\tfrac{13}{100}$.
(ii) [Allowing for two-decimal rounding of the coefficients.] If $\hat\tau_0 \in [0.035, 0.045]$ and $\hat\beta \in [-0.855, -0.845]$, then $\Delta(0.20) \in [-0.136, -0.124]$.
(iii) [Hypothesis read from Fig. 2D: the fitted control level satisfies $m_0 \in [0.222, 0.223]$.] Then $m_1(0.20) \in [0.086, 0.099]$. A number printed as $0.08$ to two decimals lies in $[0.075, 0.085]$, and $0.086 > 0.085$; so the printed $0.08$ is not the model's predicted level at 20%, and $0.095$ lies in $[0.086, 0.099]$.
(iv) [The printed numbers among themselves.] $(0.20 - 0.08)/0.20 = \tfrac35$ exactly, the printed 60% with the printed control mean $0.20$.
(v) [The printed 60% is not refuted.] Under (ii) and the hypothesis of (iii), the relative reduction $-\Delta(0.20)/m_0$ lies in $[\tfrac{124}{223}, \tfrac{68}{111}]$, an interval that contains both $0.57$ and $0.60$.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: Table S7 (SI p. 42), ‘Average school-level climate effects caused by anti-conflict groups, interacted with proportion of social referent seeds in the group’, whose note (transcribed in full in P037-T16) defines the two rows used here, the ‘estimated value of treatment when the group contains no Social Referents’ and ‘the first derivative of the effect size with respect to the percentage of the group that were referents’, and ends ‘A graphical version of this table is presented in Figure 2 in the main text of the paper.’ Fig. 2D (main p. 569), titled ‘Peer conflict (disciplinary records)’, plots, against the ‘Proportion of social referent seeds in anti-conflict group’ (axis ticks 0.05, 0.10, 0.15, 0.20), the ‘Control schools' predicted mean (and 95% CI)’ and the ‘Treatment schools' predicted mean (and 95% CI)’ of ‘Administrative Reports of Peer Conflict (Number of Reports per Student)’. Composition is a fraction (standing assumption (S4)). Not in the paper: the control level $m_0$ is not printed in any table; the validator reads it from the vector drawing of Fig. 2D as $m_0 = \tfrac{2239101}{10061740} = 0.2225\ldots$, and the treatment line at $0.20$ as $0.0951\ldots$ (P037-N010/v1/artifact/derivation.md, section 3; fig2-vector.json).
canonical_claim.note: P037-N010 is rated an error, Minor (ratings.json). Sol's verdict is confirmed in part, upheld on re-run; evidence type recalculation_from_source, so there is no counterexample target. Repair cost: none. A marginal target: a finding about a reported number, included because the number is a prediction of the paper's own fitted model, the correction changes that constant, and the comparison is exact interval arithmetic on Table S7's printed coefficients. What a Lean proof can certify: (i), (ii), the implications in (iii) and (v), and (iv).
